secondaryFeatures.title: s21e32: Video games are broken; Spotify is less broken; More people have been to Russia...; We actually have an alien?
secondaryFeatures.author: Unknown
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
0.0 Context setting

Thursday 29 September in Portland, Oregon, where it is dreary but also not raining. Dreary kind of implies rain? Some sort of pregnantly dreary, I suppose. Gravid with rain but not raining yet. Anticipatory.

It’s been just over a week since the last episode and I’ve got to say that every day that I haven’t written I’ve gotten more anxious about not having written. This is not generally speaking helpful because I don’t know about you, but it’s easier to write I’m not anxious. Easier to do anything, really.

I can’t remember if I mentioned, but I got invited to speak at Throughline 2027, Active Voice’s online conference. Here’s some stuff about it:

Join me February 3-5 for two days of talks, one day of workshops, and a whole season of special events centered on this year’s theme: ambiguity as opportunity. I’ll be talking about how to stay intentionally human—and humane—in the time of robots. Early-bird tickets are now on sale through November 8. Get all the details at throughlineconf.com/2027.

I mean it says I’m going to be talking about how to stay intentionally human--and humane--but I’m in the middle of tweaking the talk and also trying not to be anxious about that either. The organizers gave me this feedback about my submission:

Is there a weirder, spicier or more personal place you would go? Someplace thinkier, or that takes a long view and explores some of how we got here as a field? That maybe even ruffles some feathers in a productive way?

... which a) thanks, intimidating, b) thanks, flattered, and c) now having thoughts, thanks.

So that’s another Google Doc that’s staring me in the face.

0.1 How People Work, Live!

Last week I had Michele Tepper on and we exchanged some Strong Opinions, which are always fun, and then for me the interesting bit was where we landed on at the end where I think I feel a bit optimistic about how non-developers/product/designers/engineers are vibe-coding things in organizations?

Michele’s episode and all the other ones are up on the podcast and YouTube now; you can catch up on anywhere RSS works with your podcast app, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

Next up!

Friday 2 October at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Hillary Hartley

Hillary Hartley has spent nearly three decades helping government be simpler, faster, and better for the people who rely on it. She started out working with 30 state governments at NIC Inc., then went inside as a Presidential Innovation Fellow and co-founder of 18F, the first digital services team in the U.S. government. She later became Ontario's first Chief Digital and Data Officer, where she built the Ontario Digital Service and wrote the Simpler, Faster, Better Services Act. She was also CEO of U.S. Digital Response, a nonpartisan nonprofit helping state and local governments strengthen their tech capacity. She founded OpenPublic to coach public sector leaders and make transformation stick, and she co-chairs the FWD50 conference. She lives in Toronto with her family, their dog, and a veritable zoo of stuffed animals.

And then after that we’ve got:

  • Friday 9 October: HPW, Live! ... with Jim Ray, currently a founding member of developer relations at Bluesky
  • Friday 16 October: HPW, Live! ... with Farrah Bostic, who runs The Difference Engine
  • Friday 23 October: HPW, Live! ... with Lara Hogan, author and coach, and former VP Engineering at Kickstarter and former Director of Engineering at Etsy

Meanwhile, there’s the open How People Work... Does Happy Hour open clinic on Tuesdays at 1pm PT, where you get to bring what you’ve been thinking about and we chat about it as a small group. I’ve run three of these so far and they’ve all been fun.

1.0 Some things that caught my attention

1.1 Video games are broken

In Edge magazine, The game industry is broken – can we fix it?1, there’s an in-depth story covering the current state of the videogame industry. Some bits that caught my attention:

In 2005, Koster studied the previous decade or so of game budgets, and came to a startling conclusion: “The cost of game development goes up about 10x every decade.” In 2017, he repeated the experiment, this time tapping industry contacts to gather numbers on 250 releases spanning over three decades. This larger data set showed him the very same thing. The cost of making a triple-A console or PC game (accounting for inflation) grew from around $1 million in the mid-’90s to $10 million by 2005, and $100 million by 2015. In the blog post accompanying this research, Koster wrote: “We’re talking one-terabyte games that cost $250 million to develop by the early 2020s”. Today, Sweeney talks about “budgets beginning to hit the $250–400 million level” – figures that line up with those in internal documents that leaked from Insomniac in 2023.1

Essentially, games keep getting more expensive to make, but they don’t actually result in more revenue:

“Since around the year 2000, game budgets have literally doubled every few years,” Sweeney says. “The first Gears Of War, in 2006, cost us $12 million to make, and because we sold six million copies on Xbox, we made $100 million. It was immensely profitable. But, by the end of that generation, as we were making [2011’s] Gears Of War 3, it cost about $100 million to make – and our revenue projection was still about $120 million, because the audience wasn’t growing.”1

All that’s true apart from the live service games, where you get a game that regularly and frequently receives content updates and makes money via subscriptions and also in-game purchases. Epic’s Fortnite is an example of this, but in the article it’s clear that Epic isn’t have a good time of it either.

And all of this is against the backdrop of Microsoft seemingly having no coherent strategy for videogames other than (facetiously) “have a videogame console and lose money over time by spending a lot of money”, see The Xbox reset gets ugly2, from The Verge. (Netflix is also trying to figure out what the deal is with videogames because they’re hitting a limit on attention minutes through video, so need to figure out other valuable things to spend your time on for your subscription)

1.2 Spotify is less broken

Hey, that thing I keep complaining about3, where parents or other people looking after kids would have their end-of-year wrap-ups in streaming music services polluted by obsessive kid music (remember The Year of Moana and The Year of Frozen etc etc) because you couldn’t exclude certain genres or artists? They fixed it! Spotify now has a feature that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile4.

Hmm. People have been asking for this for years. I wonder why it suddenly came out? I mean, Spotify have had a whole bunch of other super important strategic things they’ve been working on, like making sure they own the relationship with your ears. And then video podcasts. And all of that jazz. How come they’ve suddenly got time for this? My hunch is that features like the exclude-genres-to-make-parents-more-sane have always been on the backlog (they’re not stupid, after all), they just haven’t been prioritized. So you don’t get to them unless you’ve got capacity and you really start burning through that backlog of stuff to implement.

Anyway it is by pure coincidence that I happened to read about Spotify’s infrastructure for scaling AI coding agents5 last month. You would be unsurprised to learn that Spotify think they’re doing super great at scaling out agentic coding infrastructure:

The organizations that learn fastest, that compound their engineering knowledge into shared, structured systems rather than leaving it scattered across individuals, will be the ones that capture the full value of AI-assisted development. We have proven that pattern at scale. Now we're shipping that expertise to you.5

If you are the kind of person who is trying to avoid using AI-generated/assisted code, I’m afraid we’re in a post-low-background steel environment6, where ever since we started testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere the background radiation has been, uh “above normal”. (Don’t worry! It is only slightly above normal now, compared to more than slightly above normal!). There’s a bunch of applications where you want steel to, like, not be that radioactive, so it’s been kind of difficult getting hold of it. People started using the low-background steel analogy a few years ago when ChatGPT came out because it came clear that the internet was going to be poisoned forever by LLM-generated material. Surprise! It has been!

1.3 More people have been to Russia than I have

Yeah, that sentence doesn’t make any sense. Sorry if it broke your brain. I discovered comparative illusion/escher sentences a while back and now you get to see them too.

Caught my attention because: you’re kidding, right?

1.4 We actually have an alien?

I am a big fan of the author Max Barry, especially Company, Jennifer Government, and Lexicon, but most recently via Metafilter7 I cam across Barry’s short story It Came from Cruden Farm published by Slate’s future tense8 which you should read because, well. I cannot give it away. But it was fun. And not fun. I won’t say any more.

That’s it for today! I’m clearly finding it a bit harder to write after a very productive spell. But this episode isn’t really what I thought it was going to be about, either. I suppose this is just how the words come out.

How have you been?

Best,

Dan

  3. Pulling the Cord; Do Not Reply; Fast User Switching — things (archive.is), me, 11 March 2024 ↩

  4. Reclaim Your Wrapped: You Can Now Control Whether Kids and Family Music Shapes Your Recommendations — Spotify (archive.is), Spotify Newsroom, 15 September 2026 ↩

  5. What we've learned scaling AI coding agents at Spotify | Spotify Portal (archive.is), Tyson Singer, Spotify, 10 August 2026 ↩↩

  6. Low-background steel - Wikipedia (archive.is), Wikipedia ↩

  7. "The alien [...] and Trump. They didn’t see eye to eye.” | MetaFilter (archive.is), Metafilter, 20 September 2026 ↩

  8. “It Came From Cruden Farm,” a new short story by Max Barry. (archive.is), Max Barry, Slate/future tense, 29 February 2020 (29 February?!) ↩

secondaryFeatures.title: THE RISE OF THE CREATOR-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX
secondaryFeatures.author: Jim
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
This Week: Creators spent the last 25 years bypassing the middlemen and the gatekeepers.  Now that they’ve arrived, a new layer is being built around them, capturing value and telling them what to produce.  What could possibly go wrong?

And please welcome my new newsletter sponsor Navan Edge.  Their AI business travel assistant helps you plan and book flights, hotels, and local restaurants in one conversation, along with a human concierge available on demand too.  Want to support this always-free newsletter?  Give Navan Edge a try here.

Hi, I’m Jim Louderback and this is my weekly creator economy newsletter. This newsletter was originally sent to email subscribers. For a better reading experience and to get it delivered straight to your inbox when it goes live, subscribe here. 

TOP STORIES

SLOPPERTAINMENT ARRIVES WITH A THUD

And all this time I was worried about AI displacing hordes of human creators.  That still could happen, but the more immediate risk?  AI-induced blandness.

Instagram and YouTube are increasingly using AI and their proprietary performance data to help creators figure out what to make.  And now TikTok has joined YouTube and ShopMy in building systems that identify successful creator content and turns it into paid media for brands.

Turns out creators have a new AI fear to go along with being put out of business.  When AI tells you what to make, measures whether you got it right, and rewards the winners with brand and affiliate dollars, you run the risk of human-generated but AI-directed mediocrity.  

Or sloppertainment.  Starring you, but inspired, packaged and sold via AI.

The bad news?  AI creates a sea of human-produced sameness.  The good news?  Weird, wacky, unexpected and unabashed human creativity still has an opportunity to break through.  Just don’t expect the optimization machines to encourage it. (TikTok)

WHY YOUTUBE FEELS THREATENED BY NETFLIX

For most of its history, YouTube had a unique and brilliant business model… creators made the video, took all the risks and only got paid after a video performed.  That business model is now changing, as YouTube is giving out multimillion-dollar exclusivity packages to top creators upfront.

 Top media analyst @Rich Greenfield explains that it’s about retaining top advertisers today and maintaining strategic relevance in the future.  Most advertisers can’t or won’t keep track of more than a handful of creator hitmakers, and if the biggest ones show up on other platforms that weakens YouTube’s market power.

Greenfield also explores why Netflix flip-flopped from disparaging many creators as simply “snackable content” in 2025 to spending (according to Greenfield) perhaps a billion dollars to lock down back catalogs and exclusives.  It’s all about engagement, something Netflix and traditional streamers desperately need more of.  Greenfield’s piece puts media’s war over creators into context, along with looking into the future of TV, streamers, YouTube and why creators should be worried too.  (LightShed Partners)

SPOTIFY RENTS ROGAN

The podcast world was abuzz with the announcement about Spotify renewing its deal with Joe Rogan, estimated for three years at about $82M a year.  Spotify gets no exclusivity or IP ownership, but will handle ad sales and licensing. That’s a lot of mid-roll ads, sponsorships and new subscribers.  With commissions and overhead Spotify will need to gross $100M or more on this show alone to avoid taking a loss. 

It’s also risky, as Rogan could be “cancelled” at any time…  leading to a flight of A-list brands from the podcast.  But the PR halo is massive, and a marquee property like Rogan gives Spotify considerable leverage when packaging inventory across the rest of its podcast business because if you want Joe, you might have to take Tom and George and Jenny too. 

Why no exclusivity?  In a world of liquid content, controlling everywhere something appears matters less than controlling advertising rights, licensing and other commercial opportunities.  

Podcaster Guy Raz is doing another interesting version of this.  He now owns “How I Built This” outright while Vox Media supplies sales, marketing, distribution, ops and live-event support.   (Yahoo, Vox Media)

THE RISE OF THE CREATOR-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX

There’s a through-line to most everything in this issue, including the three stories above: The creator economy killed the middleman, but now new middlemen are emerging, combining management, affiliate networks, creator agencies, commerce, IP sales and AI-directed show-running and monetization.  Creators were under the radar for the last 25 years, but now that they have “arrived,” new infrastructure is being hastily assembled to help brands and platforms extract maximum value from their creativity.  The term “Creator-Industrial Complex” has been around for a while, but now it has impact, with creators at the center but not necessarily at the top.

In some ways this is good, as it should lift creators of all types and increase the opportunities for building and exiting.  But I worry about who owns what, and whether an increasingly powerful layer of agencies, platforms, commerce networks and AI systems will capture an outsized share of the economics and creative decision-making too.  

Will it be more like Raz and Rogan, or will the pressure to perform for brands encourage a stifling sameness that boxes out weirdly experimental creativity… thus turning creators into fungible widgets, ultimately devalued as packaging, productizing and pitching take center stage?  

This is happening seemingly everywhere, all at once.  

Here are a few more developments from last week, all reinforcing the trend.

  • Fox adds franchise and IP development talent to its creator studio with the addition of @Bryan Thoensen and @Kirsten McAuliffe.   Forget putting YouTubers on TV, Fox is rebuilding traditional media infrastructure around creator-native content.  (Fox)
  • Axel Springer-owned Morning Brew acquired two-person creator startup Express Checkout last week.  Nice to see super-small startups attracting the attention… and ultimately the dollars… of established media companies.  Also nice: A B2B creator newsletter gets acquired.  (Dealroom)
  • SAMY acquires social agency Get Engaged for “low nine figures”, as it tries to build a global creator/social stack for brands through consolidation. (SAMY)
  • The Team (née Wasserman) acquired UK creator agency Outreach Talent Group, extending a creator representation business it has already expanded through multiple acquisitions. Another piece of evidence that creator management itself is becoming a consolidation play. (THR)
  • Also relevant: Live Nation / Creator Nation and WME’s new Creator Labs, both announced two weeks ago.

Travel Upgrade… Real-world tips from decades of business travel.

I’ve spent most of my career on the road, have achieved million-miler status on two different carriers and learned that better business travel usually comes down to two things: knowing the right shortcuts and having the right tools.

First up, I hate to wait. Lines make me crazy, so one of my favorite airport upgrades has nothing to do with TSA Pre (which you should absolutely get if you don’t have it)… it’s about knowing your airport.

At SFO, for example, if you’re flying United from the F gates early in the morning, don’t just head to the main security checkpoint in Terminal 3. Use the International Terminal instead. The checkpoint opens at 5:30am and it’s dramatically shorter for the first few hours. Once you are through it’s an easy walk to the F gates. 

Become a student of your home airport and learn its quirks. You’ll often save more time than those clever, expensive services that promise to help you jump the queue.

But not every business traveler has years to learn those shortcuts. And researching every airport, hotel, restaurant and loyalty program isn’t anyone’s idea of relaxing.

Navan Edge is my ultimate upgrade… an AI business travel assistant in your pocket that helps you plan and book flights, hotels, and local restaurants in one conversation. It learns how you like to travel, books your itinerary, and optimizes for the loyalty programs you care about (while earning you those points and miles). And when you need an actual person for a special request or dealing with disruptions, there’s a human concierge available too. Give it a try here.

FIREHOSE

@Evan Shapiro and @Shira Lazar release a comprehensive map of the “Creator Ecosphere”, with top 50 creators across 11 platforms, ranging from Facebook to X, and then top 32 subreddits and “Indie Creators”.  It’s useful in a bedazzled “wow” sort of way, and although it’s hard to peruse, interesting takeaways emerge, along with low-grade eye-strain.  First, almost all of LinkedIn’s top creators are companies, apart from Microsoft-related celebs and 3 others…  Bill Gates is #2, his ex Melinda comes in at #48, with Satya Nadella and Jeff Weiner sandwiched in between.  An apparently curated list of companies, tools, podcast platforms, and other sundry players are scattered about as well.  I enjoyed contemplating its massiveness for a bit (after downloading and mega-zooming the image). You can find the map and an explainer here. (Eshap)

RESEARCH

ANALYZING HEALTH CREATORS

Pew is known for their surveys, but their latest release is more of a census.  It analyzed more than half a million Instagram, TikTok and YouTube posts from 6,334 US health and wellness influencers to see what they are telling their audiences.

Overall, it’s all about selling.  38% of the posts pitched something and a third of creators do it in most of their posts.  Almost all (92%) pitch stuff at least occasionally.  Supplements got the most juice, as 66% of those posts were selling something.  And self-proclaimed dieticians and nutritionists were the biggest pitchers, with 43% of posts talking about a product or service.

They also found that less than 1 in 10 posts cite sources, and when they did, 4 in 10 also warned of health problems.  And only 3% of the posts analyzed came from YouTube, so this is pretty much an IG and TT study.  Looking for an underserved area of the market?  Men’s health made up just 1% of all posts, and longevity just 2%.  But don’t just post and promote.  Nearly a third of all posts wandered into the personal.  Humanity still matters.  (Pew)

QUIBIS

PLATFORMS

  • Reinforcing the Walled Garden: Meta stopped selling ads to ByteDance, and to any advertiser whose ads link to TikTok.  This is another sign of a mature market where stealing share and protecting the core becomes more important than growth.  It also brings creators, agencies and brands into the Meta vs. TikTok spat.  (Yahoo)
  • Tastes Awful, Less Filling:  The new “The Social Reckoning” movie about Facebook and Zuck is not good.  And that’s too bad for all of us. This hilariously scathing review from @Morgan Ward rips it to pieces.  (Bones Syndrome)
  • Slop Down 40%:  That’s the word from LinkedIn’s head of marketing, @Jessica Jensen, at Yahoo’s New Media Summit last week.  Turns out the new AI slop button, along with internal tools, is making a big difference.  I was wrong about thinking that button would just make people feel good.  Turns out it impacts behavior too. (LinkedIn)
  • Placebo Effect: TikTok gave thousands of users, including kids, a placebo version of a safety tool that did not work, according to New York’s attorney general.  How can we trust that it won’t do it again?  (TNW)
  • YouTube to Sony: Top YouTube OG exec @Fede Goldenberg heads to Sony to run its Screen Gems division and expand it into digital-native storytellers… aka creators. (THR)
  • How Can I Miss You If You Won’t Go Away: Unsurprisingly, employees at the new TikTok USDS JV still work regularly with global employees, and still use ByteDance’s internal Slack-type system Lark.  (Politico)

OTHER CREATOR ECONOMY

  • Spread the Wealth:  @Ezra Cooperstein thinks day-and-date licensing of a broad spectrum of YouTubers is coming.  But how much will be enough for each platform?  (LinkedIn)
  • Microdrama Consolidation?  Looks like two of the top Chinese-funded microdrama companies are merging.  A global powerhouse is about to be born.  (Wenwen Han)
  • Roll Your Own Microdrama:  When AI hands you lemons, make lemonade.  That’s what China’s AI microdrama production capital, Hengdian, is doing now that AI has swept human production out the door.  It’s turned all those wonderful locations into tourist hotspots, where for a few bucks you can star in your own Microdrama episode!  (Wenwen Han)
  • Event Powerhouse Expands: Informa reorgs and buys Clarion Events.  That means Creator Economy Live joins VidCon and Lions inside the same company…  along with IFA and more.  Content, creators, brands, creativity, tech and more all under one event umbrella.  (Informa)
  • Peak Creator Conference:  @Phil Ranta bemoans the fact that there’s a creator conference every 34 hours, while reflecting on his time at VidSummit.  His best advice…  event triage.  But whatever you do, don’t miss the 1 Billion Followers Summit (Phil will be there).  (The Creator Rep)
  • $100 Million Dreams:  @Dhar Mann announced a $100M creator/brand deal target for last week’s Advertising Week New York.  But Tubefilter says none of the deals are inked and none of the brands were named.  Love the pledge, looking forward to the evidence.  Also, Mann’s takeover of Advertising Week is just the sort of “Plus Creator” strategy that every event should build.  (Tubefilter)
  • We’re Number 2:  Congrats to QVC President @Alex Wellen for guiding their TikTok shop to the #2 biggest in the US in September ($12.11M).  Turns out you can teach an old dog new tricks…  and in this case faster than the new dogs can learn them.  (Net Influencer)
  • Fact-Checking Rules: @Syd Cohen explains why fact-checking matters, and shares best practices from top factual YouTube channels.  (Publish Press)

CREATOR TECH

  • Creators Win Round 1: A lawsuit filed by YouTubers alleging that Apple circumvented YouTube’s protections to scrape their videos can proceed, ruled a federal judge on Friday. The videos were allegedly used to train AI, but that’s not the point. The suit ignores copyright infringement and instead invokes the DMCA to collect damages.  This is the third time that a judge has let this DMCA claim continue, so worth watching for the developing precedent. (Media Post)
  • AI Fake Detector Goes Global: Google rolls out its SynthID Detector globally in English, to help anyone check whether media was made with Google’s (or its partners’) AI. It’s not perfect… it only detected AI across about 20% of my AI-Jim videos… but nailed all of the audio. (Google, SynthID)

Where’s Jim? Missed you at SF Tech Week last week. I only stopped by one event, where I was moderating a panel… family issues kept me away otherwise.  But the New Media Summit, put on by Yahoo and @Ollie New Economies was awesome.  I moderated a panel of three amazing trailblazers (@Joanna Stern, @Lillian Xu, @Sona Iliffe-Moon) sandwiched in between the President of TBPN and LinkedIn’s CMO.  What a lineup.  

Can’t wait for my first live Sharks game tomorrow at the Tank, perhaps I’ll see you there!  Go Sharks and go creators too.

Drop me an email and check out our sponsorship information here.

Like this free newsletter?  Buy me a coffee and say thanks!  Or let’s do a meetup in your town.

100% written by me. AI was used for light editing, grammar and spelling mistakes… and challenging my assumptions. AI liberally used for the illustrations and cover art.

I’ve built and sold multiple creator economy startups to top media companies… including an MCN to Discovery and VidCon to Paramount. Subscribe here  to get this newsletter every Monday in your inbox!

Let me know what you think… email me at jim@louderback.com. Thanks for reading and see you around the internet. 

DISCLAIMER: I am just one person, sharing his opinion. I do not have a team of analysts or corporate comms to check everything. I am almost definitely wrong about some of the stuff I say. My opinion is subject to change. This is not legal advice, investment advice, or anything else except hopefully some perspective that you may not have considered before.

About this newsletter. Inside the Creator Economy (ICE) is a weekly newsletter by Jim Louderback covering the business of digital creators, social media platforms, AI disruption, creator commerce, media research and creator monetization. It’s published at ICENewsletter.com and distributed via Beehiiv, LinkedIn and the blog. Jim Louderback is a creator economy journalist, former VidCon executive and early MCN pioneer who sold an MCN to Discovery and VidCon to Paramount.

Issue date. October 12, 2026.

Top stories this issue. The rise of the creator-industrial complex: agencies, studios, commerce networks and AI rebuild the middle layer around creators | Sloppertainment: TikTok joins YouTube and ShopMy in turning winning creator content into paid media | Why YouTube feels threatened by Netflix, per LightShed’s Rich Greenfield | Spotify renews Joe Rogan on a non-exclusive deal | Pew Research Center’s study of health and wellness influencer posts.

Key questions this issue answers.

What is the creator-industrial complex? The creator-industrial complex is the new layer of agencies, affiliate networks, commerce platforms, IP studios and AI tools forming around creators, according to Jim Louderback. Creators spent 25 years bypassing gatekeepers. Now that they’ve arrived, Louderback argues, this layer is being assembled to help brands and platforms capture value from creator work, with creators at the center but not necessarily at the top.

Which creator economy deals happened in early October 2026? Madrid-based SAMY agreed to acquire US creator agency Get Engaged in a deal Adweek reported at low nine figures (October 6, 2026). The Team, formerly Wasserman, bought UK creator agency Outreach Talent Group (The Hollywood Reporter, October 2026). Axel Springer-owned Morning Brew bought Express Checkout, a creator-led CPG industry newsletter from Nate Rosen and Jenna Movsowitz (Dealroom, October 5, 2026). Fox Creator Studios hired Bryan Thoensen and Kirsten McAuliffe to build creator-led franchises (Fox, October 5, 2026).

What is sloppertainment? Sloppertainment is Louderback’s term for human-made content directed by AI, which tells creators what to make, measures it and pays the winners. TikTok’s AI advertiser updates, announced at Advertising Week New York on October 5, 2026, include GMV Max and Smart+ Creative Selection, which pull creator content into automated ad campaigns (TikTok). Louderback expects a sea of human-produced sameness, with room for weird human creativity to break through.

Why is YouTube paying creators for exclusivity? According to LightShed Partners analyst Rich Greenfield (October 9, 2026), YouTube’s upfront exclusivity deals with top creators protect its hold on advertisers and its strategic relevance as Netflix and other streamers chase creator engagement. That reverses YouTube’s old model, where creators took the risk and got paid after a video performed.

What changed in Joe Rogan’s Spotify deal? Spotify renewed its multi-year licensing deal with Joe Rogan on October 8, 2026, and The Joe Rogan Experience stays non-exclusive, so it’s available on other platforms too (Music Business Worldwide, October 9, 2026). Louderback argues that in a world of liquid content, controlling advertising and licensing rights matters more than controlling where a show appears. He points to Guy Raz, who owns “How I Built This” outright while Vox Media handles sales, distribution and live events (Vox Media, September 29, 2026).

What do health and wellness influencers post? Pew Research Center analyzed 535,512 Instagram, TikTok and YouTube posts from 6,334 US health and wellness influencers, collected February 1 to April 30, 2026 (Pew Research Center, October 7, 2026). 38% of posts promoted a product or service. A third of influencers promote something in most of their posts, and 92% promote at least occasionally. Only 9% of posts cite an outside source when making a health claim. Men’s health shows up in 1% of posts and longevity in 2%.

Can anyone use Google’s SynthID Detector? Yes. Google made SynthID Detector available globally in English on October 7, 2026. Anyone can check whether an image, video or audio file came from Google’s AI or partners such as OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao (Google). It reads SynthID watermarks, so it won’t flag AI content made with tools outside that group.

Research covered. Pew Research Center, “What do health and wellness influencers post about?” (October 7, 2026). Louderback reads it as a market built on selling, with underserved niches in men’s health and longevity.

Creator economy trends mentioned. Creator economy consolidation, creator agency acquisitions, sloppertainment, creator content as paid media, YouTube exclusivity deals, non-exclusive podcast deals, creator IP ownership, day-and-date licensing, microdrama consolidation, creator conference saturation, TikTok Shop, AI scraping lawsuits under the DMCA, AI content detection, LinkedIn’s fight against AI slop, the Meta and TikTok rivalry, kids’ safety on TikTok.

Platforms and companies referenced. YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Meta, ShopMy, Netflix, LightShed Partners, Spotify, Vox Media, Fox, Fox Creator Studios, Morning Brew, Axel Springer, Express Checkout, SAMY, Get Engaged, The Team (formerly Wasserman), Outreach Talent Group, Live Nation, Creator Nation, WME, Navan, Pew Research Center, ByteDance, LinkedIn, Yahoo, Sony Pictures, Screen Gems, Lark, Informa, Clarion Events, VidCon, Cannes Lions, IFA, Creator Economy Live, VidSummit, 1 Billion Followers Summit, Advertising Week New York, Tubefilter, QVC, TikTok Shop, Net Influencer, The Publish Press, Apple, Google, Google DeepMind, SynthID, TBPN.

People referenced. Jim Louderback, Rich Greenfield, Joe Rogan, Guy Raz, Bryan Thoensen, Kirsten McAuliffe, Nate Rosen, Jenna Movsowitz, Morgan Ward, Jessica Jensen, Fede Goldenberg, Ezra Cooperstein, Wenwen Han, Phil Ranta, Dhar Mann, Alex Wellen, Syd Cohen, Evan Shapiro, Shira Lazar, Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates, Satya Nadella, Jeff Weiner, Tony Robbins, Arianna Huffington, Richard Branson, Joanna Stern, Lillian Xu.

Jim Louderback’s core arguments this week. The creator economy killed the middleman, and a new set of middlemen is forming around creators that combines management, affiliate, commerce, IP sales and AI-directed showrunning. More buyers and exits help creators, but Louderback worries this layer will capture an outsized share of the economics and the creative decisions, and that AI-directed formulas will produce human-made sameness he calls sloppertainment. In a world of liquid content, controlling ad sales, licensing and IP matters more than exclusivity, which is why Rogan’s non-exclusive renewal and Guy Raz’s ownership deal with Vox Media point the way. And Meta’s ban on ads from ByteDance and ads linking to TikTok is a sign of a mature market where protecting the core matters more than growth.

secondaryFeatures.title: Abdul El-Sayed Disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood. It Didn’t Count.
secondaryFeatures.author: Parker Molloy
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
On Saturday, at a town hall in Caro, Michigan, a man named Tommy asked Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, “I have one simple question. Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” El-Sayed’s first words in reply were “Sure, yeah, absolutely.” Then he asked Tommy why he was asking that question. The two went back and forth for a few minutes, and El-Sayed posted the exchange on X that night.

The next morning, on CNN’s State of the Union, host Dana Bash played the clip for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI). “So he said, ‘Yes, sure,’” Bash began. Rogers started talking about the streamer Hasan Piker (as he has been doing throughout the campaign), then got to the video:

ROGERS: He didn’t disavow it. He goes on this word salad trying to get around the fact that he can’t do it.

BASH: He said — he did — he did say — he said, “Sure, yes.”

ROGERS: No, that’s not true. Dana, listen...

Bash pushed back, saying, “I want to be factual. He said, ‘Yes, sure,’” but Rogers kept going: “He didn’t disavow it. He didn’t say no. He didn’t say it worries me that they treat women differently under the Muslim Brotherhood’s view of Sharia law. He didn’t say any of that. He didn’t because he won’t and he can’t.” That night, the Rogers campaign put “won’t and can’t” in the headline of a press release: “MIKE ROGERS ON CNN: ABDUL WON’T AND CAN’T DISAVOW THE MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD.”
